chapter: Teaching, race and the future of jazz
title: Black children in Washington who did not know Duke
summary: Black people have no unity or church; federal school money does not reach jazz.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: Becoming a teacher: jazz in schools and conservatories

blocks.x: Because -- the school -- that leads into something else. When Mary McBrothen was doing some things with the school kids in Washington, and there the school population is about 97 percent black. And she got Duke to read and come and talk to them and play for them, and she said most of them didn't know who he was.
Black people been brainwashed, man, they're separated, they have no church. We have no church, we have no unity at all.
You got to have someplace to go, discuss about the policeman's blowing your kid's brains out. There are so many (unintelligible) now.
You got the Moslems or Muslims, they got (unintelligible) -- what is this guy?
Yeah, I know who you mean.

One of the things I was hoping for, as federal monies started coming in to a lot of the schools in the city, and some of that money is supposed to go to culture. And so far as I know, with very few exceptions, none of it has gone so that kids can learn about Duke or Billie or whatever.
